claim: High-speed videography during nociceptive Aδ fiber stimulation demonstrated engagement of a multi-segmental motor program coincident with, or even preceding, withdrawal of the stimulated paw.
source: Here, high-speed videography during nociceptive Aδ fiber stimulation demonstrated engagement of a multi-segmental motor program coincident with, or even preceding, withdrawal of the stimulated paw.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from high-speed videography observations described in the manuscript.

claim: The motor program included early head orientation and adjustments of the torso and un-stimulated paws.
source: The motor program included early head orientation and adjustments of the torso and un-stimulated paws.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from high-speed videography data.

claim: A remarkably potent gating mechanism was observed when the animal was standing on its hindlimbs.
source: Moreover, we observed a remarkably potent gating mechanism when the animal was standing on its hindlimbs and which was partially dependent on the endogenous opioid system.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing responses in different postural conditions.

claim: The gating mechanism was partially dependent on the endogenous opioid system.
source: Moreover, we observed a remarkably potent gating mechanism when the animal was standing on its hindlimbs and which was partially dependent on the endogenous opioid system.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using naloxone, an opioid antagonist.

claim: Selective thermal activation was achieved using a brief (100 ms), small-diameter (1.6 mm), and high-energy (5000 mA) infrared diode laser pulse.
source: Selective thermal activation was achieved using a brief (100 ms), small-diameter (1.6 mm), and high-energy (5000 mA) infrared diode laser pulse.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Upon forelimb stimulation in the quadrupedal stance, the rat produced an appropriate withdrawal sequence in 100% of the trials for both laser (n = 5) and sharp (n = 14) stimuli.
source: Upon forelimb stimulation, in the quadrupedal stance, the rat produced an appropriate withdrawal sequence in 100% of the trials for both laser (n = 5) and sharp (n = 14) stimuli (Figure 2A,B; see Videos 1,2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing withdrawal rates.

claim: Eighty percent (laser) to 100% (pinprick) of forepaw stimulations provoked orientation of the head toward the stimulated limb.
source: Eighty percent (laser) to 100% (pinprick) of forepaw stimulations provoked orientation of the head toward the stimulated limb.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations quantifying head movement responses.

claim: Forelimb withdrawal occurred without movement of either hindlimb following laser stimulation.
source: Despite movement of the head, forelimb withdrawal occurred without movement of either hindlimb. This was especially evident with the thermal laser pulse: neither hindlimb moved following the stimulus (Figure 2A,Ba).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from high-speed videography.

claim: Movements evoked by the sharp stimulus always occurred earlier than those evoked by the thermal stimulus by 48.3 ms and 48.1 ms for the stimulated forepaw or the head, respectively.
source: Also evident is a difference in the latency of the first movement or limb withdrawal between sharp and thermal laser stimulation. Movements evoked by the sharp stimulus always occurred earlier than those evoked by the thermal stimulus by 48.3 ms and 48.1 ms for the stimulated forepaw or the head, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of response latencies.

claim: The head and the stimulated hind paw moved at approximately the same time following both pinprick and thermal laser stimulation.
source: With both stimulus modalities, the head and the stimulated hind paw moved at approximately same time (Pinprick: Head- 52.0 ± 5.2 ms; ipsi Hind paw-51.6 ± 3.6 ms; Thermal Laser: Head- 169.9 ± 9.5 ms; ipsi Hind paw- 180.2 ± 8.1 ms).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of movement latencies.

claim: Sharp stimulation provoked a withdrawal movement within ~50 ms, whereas thermal laser stimulation caused withdrawal within ~180 ms.
source: As was observed for forepaw stimulation, there was a noticeable difference in the withdrawal latency for the two stimuli: Sharp stimulation provoked a withdrawal movement within ~50 ms, whereas thermal laser stimulation caused withdrawal within ~180 ms (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of withdrawal latencies.

claim: Processing of the stimuli into an integrated response is much more rapid with a mechanical stimulus than with a thermal stimulus.
source: Thus, processing of the stimuli into an integrated response is much more rapid with a mechanical stimulus than with a thermal stimulus, even with the very fast rate of stimulation provided by the infrared diode laser.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing different response latencies for mechanical versus thermal stimuli.

claim: Sharp stimulation of the hindlimb produced a 100% withdrawal and was preceded by twitch in 7% of the trials (n = 31).
source: Sharp stimulation of the hindlimb also produced a 100% withdrawal and was preceded by twitch in 7% of the trials (n = 31).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data quantifying withdrawal responses.

claim: Infrared thermal stimulation of the hind paw failed to produce withdrawal in 18% of the trials, with 14% showing just a twitch and 4% no movement at all.
source: In contrast, infrared thermal stimulation of the hind paw failed to produce withdrawal in 18% of the trials, with 14% showing just a twitch and 4% no movement at all (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data quantifying withdrawal responses.

claim: The earliest responses to forelimb stimulation were shorter than those for hindlimb stimulation.
source: Collectively, the data show that the earliest responses were to sharp stimuli and the slowest were to laser stimuli. The averaged first response latencies for forelimb stimulation were shorter than those for hindlimb stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A significant difference in the latencies between forelimb and hindlimb stimulation was found for the responses to laser stimulation (Forelimb: 93.9 ± 33.0 ms, n = 5; Hindlimb: 167.5 ± 43.0 ms, n = 29; p<0.0001).
source: A significant difference in the latencies between forelimb and hindlimb stimulation was found for the responses to laser stimulation (Forelimb: 93.9 ± 33.0 ms, n = 5; Hindlimb: 167.5 ± 43.0 ms, n = 29; *p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Head movement occurred nearly simultaneously and could even precede movement of the paw receiving the noxious stimulus.
source: Head movement occurred nearly simultaneously and could even precede movement of the paw receiving the noxious stimulus.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from high-speed videography.

claim: The mean latency to head movement upon sharp stimulation of the forelimb was 40.3 ± 7.0 ms and for hindlimb stimulation was 52.8 ± 5.0 ms.
source: The mean latency to head movement upon sharp stimulation of the forelimb was 40.3 ± 7.0 ms and for hindlimb stimulation was 52.8 ± 5.0 ms.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of head movement latencies.

claim: The mean latency to the start of head movement upon laser heat stimulation of the forelimb was 88.5 ± 17.0 ms and 169.9 ± 10.0 ms for the hindlimb stimulation.
source: The mean latency to the start of head movement upon laser heat stimulation of the forelimb was 88.5 ± 17.0 ms and 169.9 ± 10.0 ms for the hindlimb stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of head movement latencies.

claim: The rats were largely indifferent to the non-noxious blunt stimulus.
source: The rats were largely indifferent to this non-noxious stimulus.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of behavioral responses to blunt stimuli.

claim: The first movement (head orientation) occurred within 226.6 ± 77.0 ms and 263.6 ± 83.0 ms of pushing on the fore- or hind paw, respectively, with the blunt stimulus.
source: Nonetheless, the first movement (head orientation) occurred within 226.6 ± 77.0 ms and 263.6 ± 83.0 ms of pushing on the fore- or hind paw, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of response latencies to blunt stimuli.

claim: In 50% of the blunt trials the animals terminated the trial simply by walking away.
source: The indifference to the blunt probe is evidenced by the fact that in 50% of the blunt trials the animals terminated the trial simply by walking away.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of behavioral responses.

claim: The limb movement latencies to blunt stimuli were significantly longer than the responses to laser or the pinprick stimulus (blunt-forelimb: 308.1 ± 241.0 ms, n = 7; blunt- hindlimb: 324.1 ± 115.0 ms, n = 6).
source: The limb movement latencies were significantly longer than the responses to laser or the pinprick stimulus (blunt-forelimb: 308.1 ± 241.0 ms, n = 7; blunt- hindlimb: 324.1 ± 115.0 ms, n = 6)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical comparison of response latencies.

claim: The probability of withdrawal to blunt stimulus was substantially lower (blunt stimulus to forelimb: 57%; blunt stimulus to hindlimb: 33%).
source: and the probability of withdrawal was substantially lower (blunt stimulus to forelimb: 57%; blunt stimulus to hindlimb: 33%; no difference in the probability to respond: forelimb vs hindlimb p=0.6; Fisher Exact test; 2 × 2 contingency table for two nominal variables with expected small or zero values).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: When the animals were standing on all four limbs, they responded to a laser stimulus in 83% of the trials (n = 29) and to sharp stimulus 100% of the trials (n = 31).
source: When the animals were standing on all four limbs, they responded to a laser stimulus in 83% of the trials (n = 29) and to sharp stimulus 100% of the trials (n = 31, sharp vs laser, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data quantifying response rates.

claim: When the animals stood only on their hindlimbs, they responded to a laser stimulus in only 49% of the trials (n = 39).
source: However, when the animals stood only on their hindlimbs, they responded to a laser stimulus in only 49% of the trials (n = 39) (p<0.01; Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing postural effects on response rates.

claim: A statistical difference in the proportion of trials in which the animals responded to the sharp stimulus in the quadrupedal (n = 31) compared to the bipedal stance (n = 45) was found (100% vs. 67%, p<0.001).
source: We also found a statistical difference in the proportion of trails in which the animals responded to the sharp stimulus in the quadrupedal (n = 31) compared to the bipedal stance (n = 45) (100% vs. 67%, p<0.001; Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The latency to the onset of head or limb movements when the sharp stimulus was applied was significantly longer in the bipedal compared to the quadrupedal stance (86.3 ± 11.0 ms vs 46.9 ± 4.0 ms, respectively, p<0.005).
source: The latency to the onset of head or limb movements when the sharp stimulus was applied, was significantly longer in the bipedal compared to the quadrupedal stance (Sharp stimulus- standing on hindlimbs vs. standing on all four limbs: 86.3 ± 11.0 ms vs 46.9 ± 4.0 ms, respectively, p<0.005, Two-ways ANOVA, Tukey's multiple comparison test) (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: When the rat was in a bipedal stance, movements of the stimulated hindlimb were delayed until the forepaws came down and touched the platform.
source: When the rat was in a bipedal stance, movements of the stimulated hindlimb (twitching, withdrawal, shaking) were delayed until the forepaws came down and touched the platform.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from high-speed videography.

claim: When in the bipedal stance, the animals reacted significantly faster to sharp stimuli than to laser stimuli delivered to the hind paw (sharp vs. laser 86.3 ± 11.0 ms, n = 45 versus 150.3 ± 11.0 ms, n = 39; p≤0.0001).
source: When in the bipedal stance, the animals reacted significantly faster to sharp stimuli than to laser stimuli delivered to the hind paw (sharp vs. laser 86.3 ± 11.0 ms, n = 45 versus 150.3 ± 11.0 ms, n = 39; p≤0.0001, two-way ANOVA, Tukey's multiple comparison test; Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: At least one of the three types of inhibition (complete, delayed, or partial) occurred in ~50% of all trials administered to rats in the bipedal stance for both thermal laser and sharp stimuli.
source: At least one of the three types of inhibition occurred in ~50% of all trials administered to rats in the bipedal stance for both thermal laser and sharp stimuli.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data analyzing types of withdrawal responses.

claim: The response rate to noxious stimuli was unchanged in the presence of naloxone (laser: 63%, n = 19; sharp 55%, n = 20) when the rat was standing on its hindlimbs, compared to pre-drug control conditions.
source: Contrary to our expectation, the response rate to noxious stimuli was unchanged in the presence of naloxone (laser: 63%, n = 19; sharp 55%, n = 20, Figure 6A) when the rat was standing on its hindlimbs, compared to pre-drug control conditions (laser no drug vs. naloxone, p=0.4026; sharp no drug vs. naloxone, p>0.4; laser naloxone vs. sharp naloxone, p>0.7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing responses with and without naloxone.

claim: The presence of naloxone did not change the average withdrawal latency to thermal laser stimulation when comparing three conditions (quadrupedal, bipedal, and bipedal + naloxone).
source: The presence of naloxone also did not change the average withdrawal latency to thermal laser stimulation when comparing three conditions (quadrupedal, bipedal, and bipedal + naloxone) (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing latencies across conditions.

claim: Naloxone significantly reduced the latency to the first movement in response to the sharp stimulus (no drug, quadrupedal: 46.9 ± 4.0 ms; no drug bipedal: 86.3 ± 11.0 ms; bipedal with naloxone: 55.1 ± 7.0 ms, p<0.05).
source: However, naloxone significantly reduced the latency to the first movement in response to the sharp stimulus (no drug, quadrupedal: 46.9 ± 4.0 ms; no drug bipedal: 86.3 ± 11.0 ms; bipedal with naloxone: 55.1 ± 7.0 ms, p<0.05; Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: When a quadrupedal animal raises one limb it assumes a diagonal posture in which the weight is borne primarily by the contralateral hindlimb and the diagonal (ipsilateral) forelimb.
source: When a quadrupedal animal raises one limb it assumes a diagonal posture in which the weight is borne primarily by the contralateral hindlimb and the diagonal (ipsilateral) forelimb. This behavior was initially reported in dogs (Ioffe and Andreev, 1969); cited in Gahéry and Massion (1981) and later confirmed in cats (Coulmance et al., 1979; Massion and Gahery, 1979; Gahéry and Massion, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: When a noxious stimulus was applied to the hind paw, the sequence of movements elicited resembles a diagonal postural adjustment.
source: Consistent with these reports, when a noxious stimulus was applied to the hind paw, the sequence of movements elicited resembles a diagonal postural adjustment.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and comparison to previous research.

claim: Multiple factors may account for the latency difference between fore paw and hind paw thermal laser stimulation including the physical length of the nerve, the higher innervation density of myelinated fibers in the fore paw compared to the hind paw, and the wide range of conduction velocities for Aδ fibers.
source: Multiple factors may account for this difference including the physical length of the nerve (Mitchell et al., 2010), the higher innervation density of myelinated fibers in the fore paw compared to the hind paw (Matsumoto and Mori, 1975) and the wide range of conduction velocities for Aδ fibers (Ringkamp and Meyer, 2008; Abraira and Ginty, 2013).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The response to noxious stimulation of the forelimbs was less extensive than the responses to stimulation of the hindlimbs.
source: The response to noxious stimulation of the forelimbs was less extensive than the responses to stimulation of the hindlimbs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Sherrington showed that forelimb stimulation was much less likely to initiate movement of the hindlimbs than vice versa.
source: This is consistent with early studies of long reflexes by Sherrington who showed that forelimb stimulation was much less likely to initiate movement of the hindlimbs than vice versa (Sherrington, 1910).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The behavioral responses to noxious stimuli were dependent on the animal's posture when the stimulus was applied.
source: We found that the behavioral responses to noxious stimuli were dependent on the animal's posture when the stimulus was applied.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing responses in different postural conditions.

claim: While in the upright stance, the animal temporarily inhibited the limb responses to maintain postural stability.
source: The simplest interpretation of these findings is that, while in the upright stance, the animal temporarily inhibited the limb responses to maintain postural stability.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation inferred from experimental observations.

claim: The increase in latency to withdrawal in the bipedal stance may be due to, at least in part, to direct release of opioid peptides.
source: This result suggests that the increase latency to withdrawal in the bipedal stance may be due to, at least in part, to direct release of opioid peptides.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the naloxone experimental results.

claim: An opioidergic component to the postural inhibition is consistent with studies showing that withdrawal reflexes are under tonic inhibition by opioids which can be relieved by naloxone.
source: An opioidergic component to the postural inhibition is consistent with studies showing that withdrawal reflexes are under tonic inhibition by opioids which can be relieved by naloxone (Catley et al., 1983; Chung et al., 1983; Clarke et al., 1992; Steffens and Schomburg, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Opioids interact with multiple non-nociceptive pathways.
source: Opioids interact with multiple non-nociceptive pathways (Steffens and Schomburg, 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Opioids can modulate locomotor-like activity in the neonatal rat spinal cord.
source: and can modulate locomotor-like activity in the neonatal rat spinal cord (Blivis et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Met5-enkephalin-Arg6-Gly7-Leu8 containing immunoreactive terminals can be detected on the perikarya of motor neurons.
source: and met5-enkephalin-Arg6-Gly7-Leu8, a proenkephalin-derived met5-enkephalin-Arg6-Gly7-Leu8 containing immunoreactive terminals can be detected on the perikarya of motor neurons (Iadarola et al., 1985, 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Noxious stimuli or ventral root stimuli that initiate locomotor-like activity in the isolated spinal cord of the neonatal rat and mouse are blocked by the µ-opioid agonist DAMGO.
source: Furthermore, noxious stimuli (Blivis et al., 2007) or ventral root stimuli (D Blivis; unpublished data) that initiate locomotor-like activity in the isolated spinal cord of the neonatal rat and mouse are blocked by the µ-opioid agonist DAMGO.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research and unpublished data.

claim: The latency of the first movement is regulated by an opioid action at the spinal level that may include deep dorsal horn laminae and perhaps also the ventral cord.
source: Accordingly, we hypothesize that the latency of the first movement is regulated by an opioid action at the spinal level that may include deep dorsal horn laminae and perhaps also the ventral cord.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on experimental data and previous research.

claim: To account for the complete postural inhibition of the withdrawal response, other glycinergic and GABAergic inhibitory networks are engaged.
source: To account for the complete postural inhibition of the withdrawal response, we propose that other glycinergic and GABAergic inhibitory networks are engaged (Levine et al., 2014; Harvey et al., 2004; Foster et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is a proposal based on experimental observations and citations to relevant literature.

claim: Laser stimulation requires a minimum of ~60 ms of heating before reaching a temperature that causes paw withdrawal.
source: Laser stimulation requires a minimum of ~60 ms of heating before reaching a temperature that causes paw withdrawal (Mitchell et al., 2010, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The mechanically responsive Aδ fibers have fast conduction velocities.
source: The mechanically responsive Aδ fibers have fast conduction velocities (Ringkamp and Meyer, 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: At the molecular level, the composition of receptors and ion channels may be different between mechanically responsive and thermally responsive Aδ fibers.
source: Consistent with the idea of distinct fiber types, at the molecular level, the composition of receptors and ion channels may also be different (Goswami et al., 2014; Usoskin et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The preponderance of neuro-anatomical data indicates that the connections between the superficial laminae to the deeper laminae is not direct.
source: Although the preponderance of neuro-anatomical data indicates that the connections between the superficial laminae to the deeper laminae is not direct (Cui et al., 2016; Hilde et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A set of interneurons in medial deep dorsal horn coordinate the execution of compound movements across multiple joints.
source: A set of interneurons in medial deep dorsal horn that meet many of the criteria delineated above appears to coordinate the execution of compound movements across multiple joints.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from previous research.

claim: This region was a nexus for multimodal inputs from various muscle groups, cortico-spinal tract neurons, proprioceptive afferents, and, via synaptic relay, nociceptive afferent inputs.
source: This region was also a nexus for multimodal inputs from various muscle groups, cortico-spinal tract neurons, proprioceptive afferents, and, via synaptic relay, nociceptive afferent inputs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from previous research.

claim: This heterogeneous population of neurons expresses the DNA-binding protein Satb1 and Satb2.
source: This heterogeneous population of neurons expresses the DNA-binding protein Satb1 and Satb2 and is in a region of the dorsal horn that has previously been shown to contain neurons regulating limb withdrawal reflexes in the rat (Schouenborg et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The Satb1 neurons are inhibitory and comprise both GABA- and glycinergic neurons.
source: The Satb1 neurons are inhibitory and comprise both GABA- and glycinergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from previous research.

claim: Satb1 neurons receive monosynaptic input from muscle spindle afferents and indirect inputs from nociceptors and cutaneous afferents and project to motoneurons and V1 and V2A interneurons.
source: They receive monosynaptic input from muscle spindle afferents and indirect inputs from nociceptors and cutaneous afferents and project to motoneurons and V1 and V2A interneurons (Hilde et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: When Satb2 is genetically deleted from these inhibitory interneurons their development and connectivity are severely perturbed resulting in animals with exaggerated withdrawal reflexes to noxious stimuli.
source: When Satb2 is genetically deleted from these inhibitory interneurons their development and connectivity are severely perturbed resulting in animals with exaggerated withdrawal reflexes to noxious stimuli (Hilde et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: These neurons may account for the postural inhibitory, non-opioid control of withdrawal reflexes and may participate in retention of the animal's balance and posture.
source: We hypothesize that these neurons may account for the postural inhibitory, non-opioid control of withdrawal reflexes and may participate in retention of the animal's balance and posture.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on experimental data and previous research.

claim: Early Ret+ dorsal horn neurons are mainly involved with sensory gating of nociceptive transmission to the spino-thalamic projection neurons.
source: This study anatomically and functionally defines a set of early Ret+ dorsal horn neurons mainly involved with sensory gating of nociceptive transmission to the spino-thalamic projection neurons (Cui et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Spino-bulbo-spinal descending control mechanisms in rostral medulla have been implicated in monitoring ongoing sensory input and modifying withdrawal reflexes in the event of a painful stimulus.
source: Spino-bulbo-spinal descending control mechanisms in rostral medulla have been implicated in monitoring ongoing sensory input and modifying withdrawal reflexes in the event of a painful stimulus (Hellman and Mason, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: There are two gating mechanisms in the dorsal horn: one in the more superficial laminae that gates the access of primary afferent nociceptive input to spinothalamic projection neurons, and another in the deeper dorsal horn that gates the access of primary afferent nociceptive information to the motor apparatus.
source: Integration of the present findings with the above-cited studies in mouse, suggests that there are two gating mechanisms in the dorsal horn. One is in the more superficial laminae and gates the access of primary afferent nociceptive input to spinothalamic projection neurons, thereby modulating the relay of noxious sensory information from the cord to the brain. The other is in the deeper dorsal horn and gates the access of primary afferent nociceptive information to the motor apparatus, thereby conferring the capability for integration of the response with the ongoing and planned motor activity.
evidence: The claim is an inference integrating the present findings with previous research.

claim: Male Sprague-Dawley rats (250–350 g; N = 9) were used in the study.
source: Male Sprague-Dawley rats (250–350 g; N = 9) were housed under a 12/12 hr light-dark cycle and allowed access to food and water ad libitum.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: Thermal stimuli were generated by an infrared diode laser (LASS-10 M; Lasmed, LLC, Mountain View, CA) with an output wavelength of 980 nm and maximum power of 20 W.
source: Thermal stimuli (i.e. 'Laser') were generated by an infrared diode laser (LASS-10 M; Lasmed, LLC, Mountain View, CA) with an output wavelength of 980 nm and maximum power of 20 W.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental equipment and methods used.

claim: Aδ-fibers were selectively activated with a high rate of heating, using a high-energy (5000–5500 mA), brief pulse (100 ms), and a small spot size (1.6 mm Ø, nominal).
source: Aδ -fibers were selectively activated with a high rate of heating, using a high-energy (5000–5500 mA), brief pulse (100 ms), and a small spot size (1.6 mm Ø, nominal).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology for selective fiber activation.

claim: At 5000 mA (5.12 W/mm2) the rate of infrared laser diode heating was ~235 °C/s and no thermal damage to the skin was observed.
source: At 5000 mA (5.12 W/mm2) the rate of infrared laser diode heating was ~235 °C/s and no thermal damage to the skin was observed (e.g. we did not observe the presence of protein coagulation, acute redness, blistering or swelling at 24 hr post stimulation) (Mitchell et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and citation to previous research.

claim: A high-speed 12-bit monochrome camera (AOS Technologies AG, Switzerland) was used to record limb and head movements before, during, and after the stimulus.
source: To further quantify and characterize this sequence of events, we used a high-speed 12-bit monochrome camera (AOS Technologies AG, Switzerland) to record limb and head movements before, during, and after the stimulus.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental equipment used for data collection.

claim: Initially, images were acquired at 500 frames per second (fps) but additional experiments showed that 130–170 fps could capture the time course of the behavioral sequence with sufficient temporal resolution.
source: Initially, images were acquired at 500 frames per second (fps) but additional experiments showed that 130–170 fps could capture the time course of the behavioral sequence with sufficient temporal resolution.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methodology and optimization.

claim: The two-way ANOVA analysis had a power of 0.92 for the results presented in Figure 3 and 0.71 for the results presented in Figure 6B.
source: A post-hoc power analysis was done using G-Power 3.1.9.2. The two-way ANOVA analysis had a power of 0.92 for the results presented in Figure 3 and 0.71 for the results presented in Figure 6B.
evidence: The claim describes the statistical power analysis performed on the data.
